pos: n. (Johann Heinrich Heidegger, 1633–1698, Zurich theologian and principal author of the Helvetic Consensus)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Germanic Heinrich, home-ruler; Heidegger, dweller on the heath.
biblical_def: Johann Heinrich Heidegger taught theology at Zurich for more than thirty years and wrote the first draft of the Formula Consensus Helvetica of 1675, the last confessional document the Swiss Reformed churches produced together. It was written against the teaching coming out of the French academy at Saumur: that Christ died for all men conditionally, that the imputation of Adam's guilt is mediate rather than immediate, and that the Hebrew vowel points and the received text of the Old Testament are not themselves the preserved word. Heidegger also produced a large body of dogmatics and biblical history, including a handbook of the covenant theology. The dictionary values the Formula and names what it cost. It was a careful, limited, confessional answer to a real softening, and within two generations the Swiss cantons had abandoned it under pressure from the courts and the universities. A church may be perfectly right in its confession and still fail to keep it, and the Formula's short life is a warning rather than a defeat.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines formula as a prescribed form of words, and consensus as agreement of minds.
webster_full: FOR'MULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; a stated form of words.
CONSENT', n. Agreement of minds in opinion; accord; concord.
IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; the reckoning of guilt or righteousness to another.
DOGMAT'ICS, n. The doctrinal system of divinity set forth in order.
scriptures: Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
Psa 12:7

corruption_summary: He drafted the Helvetic Consensus of 1675 against Saumur, and saw the cantons abandon it within two generations.
corruption_paragraphs: The errors the Formula was written against should be named as it named them. The Saumur theology taught a universal conditional decree of redemption, so that Christ's death purchased salvation for all on condition of faith rather than actually securing the salvation of the elect; it taught that Adam's guilt reaches us only through our inherited corruption rather than being immediately reckoned to us; and it treated the Hebrew vowel points and the received Old Testament text as late and uncertain. Each softening looks small and each moves the ground: the first makes the atonement indefinite, the second makes original guilt derivative, and the third makes the text an object of reconstruction.

The standard is the text. Imputation is immediate and representative: “For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). The atonement is definite in its object: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15). And the words of God are preserved, not merely once given: “The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times” (Psa 12:6), and “Thou shalt keep them, O LORD, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever” (Psa 12:7).

pos: n. (Lucas Gernler, 1625–1675, antistes of Basel and co-author of the Helvetic Consensus)
etymology: Greek Loukas, of Lucania; Germanic Gernler, a Swiss surname.
biblical_def: Lucas Gernler was professor of theology and then antistes — chief pastor — of the church at Basel, and with Heidegger of Zurich and Francis Turretin of Geneva he was one of the three men chiefly responsible for the Formula Consensus Helvetica. His part was to carry Basel, which had the most independent of the Swiss theological faculties and the most to lose from a tight subscription, and he did it. He died the year the Formula was adopted. The dictionary records him as the man who did the persuading. A confession has an author and it also has the men who go from city to city getting magistrates and faculties to sign, and the second labour is usually the harder. Gernler spent the last years of a short life travelling between Swiss cantons arguing that a softening in France was a danger in Switzerland, which is the sort of argument nobody thanks a man for making.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines antistes as a chief priest or presiding minister, and subscribe as to attest by writing one's name beneath.
webster_full: AN'TISTES, n. A chief or presiding minister; among the Swiss Reformed, the chief pastor of a city church.
SUBSCRI'BE, v.t. To attest by writing the name beneath; to assent to.
FAC'ULTY, n. The body of professors or instructors in a university or one of its departments.
CAN'TON, n. A small division of territory, as the cantons of Switzerland.

corruption_summary: He carried Basel for the Helvetic Consensus and died the year it was adopted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a doctrinal danger abroad is somebody else's business. Basel had no quarrel with Saumur and no immediate trouble of its own; Gernler's argument was that an error allowed anywhere in the Reformed communion will arrive everywhere in a generation, and the century that followed proved him right in the worst way.

The principle to recover is that contending for the faith is a corporate duty, and that churches owe one another plain speech. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The pattern is to be held and not improvised: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13). And the model of a church speaking with one voice is the Jerusalem letter: “It seemed good unto us, being assembled with one accord” (Act 15:25).

pos: n. (Johann Heinrich Hottinger, 1620–1667, Zurich orientalist and church historian)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Germanic Heinrich, home-ruler; Hottinger, of Hottingen near Zurich.
biblical_def: Johann Heinrich Hottinger was a Zurich pastor's son who learned Hebrew, Aramaic, Syriac and Arabic, studied in the Netherlands, and came home to teach oriental languages and church history at Zurich for a quarter of a century. He wrote a nine-volume ecclesiastical history, grammars and lexicons of the Semitic tongues, a survey of what Europe then knew of the Islamic world drawn from Arabic sources, and a bibliography of oriental literature. He was drowned with three of his children in the Limmat while crossing by boat, at forty-seven, on his way to take up a chair at Leiden. The dictionary names him as a particular kind of servant. Hottinger learned four difficult languages so that the Old Testament could be read better and the eastern churches understood from their own writings rather than from rumour, and the whole of that labour was undertaken in the conviction that the text is the thing and the text is in Hebrew.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oriental as eastern, and philology as the study of language and literature.
webster_full: ORIENT'AL, a. Eastern; proceeding from the east; as the oriental tongues.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words; criticism; that branch of literature which comprehends a knowledge of the etymology of words.
LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary of the words in a language.
ECCLESIAS'TICAL, a. Pertaining to the church; as ecclesiastical history.
scriptures: Dan 1:17
As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.
Act 22:3

I am verily a man which am a Jew, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, yet brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers, and was zealous toward God, as ye all are this day.
Pro 2:4
If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures;
Col 2:3

corruption_summary: He learned four Semitic tongues for the Old Testament's sake and drowned at forty-seven on his way to Leiden.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a pious shortcut: the belief that since the Spirit teaches, the languages are optional, so that the church may rely indefinitely on translations made by men who did take the trouble. Hottinger took the trouble, and his lexicons served three generations of preachers who could therefore check their text.

The principle to recover is that God gives such learning as a gift and expects it to be dug for. “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom” (Dan 1:17). Wisdom is to be sought like buried treasure: “If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Pro 2:4). Paul's own training is stated without apology — “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, and taught according to the perfect manner of the law of the fathers” (Act 22:3) — and the end of all such searching is Christ, “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3).

pos: n. (Johann Caspar Suicer, 1620–1684, Zurich scholar, compiler of the Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Persian through Latin Caspar, treasurer; Suicer, latinised from Schweizer, a Swiss.
biblical_def: Johann Caspar Suicer spent his working life on one book. The Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus is a lexicon of the Greek used by the church fathers, assembled word by word out of the Greek patristic writings, showing what each theological term meant to the men who used it in the first five centuries. It was published in 1682 and is still consulted. Suicer taught Greek and Hebrew at Zurich and Heidelberg and wrote little else of note. The dictionary gives him an entry precisely because of that single-mindedness. Doctrinal controversy constantly turns on what an old word meant — whether a father who used a term meant by it what a modern party means — and the only way to settle such a question is to have the evidence collected. Suicer collected it, and in doing so armed the Reformed against the claim that the fathers were on Rome's side, without asserting anything about the fathers that the fathers' own words would not bear.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thesaurus as a treasury or repository, and patristic as pertaining to the ancient fathers of the church.
webster_full: THESAU'RUS, n. A treasury; a repository; a collection of words or of knowledge.
PATRIS'TIC, a. Pertaining to the ancient fathers of the Christian church.
GLOSS'ARY, n. A dictionary or vocabulary explaining obscure or antiquated words.
ETYMOL'OGY, n. That part of philology which explains the origin and derivation of words.

Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.

corruption_summary: His patristic Greek lexicon let the fathers be read in their own words rather than quoted in a party's favour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is proof-texting the fathers — mining the first five centuries for sentences that sound like one's own position, a method practised with enthusiasm by Rome, by the Reformed, and now by anyone with a search engine. Suicer's lexicon is the cure and not the disease: it shows what a word actually did in patristic usage, which makes selective quotation harder for everybody.

The principle to recover is that antiquity is evidence and Scripture is the rule. “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The Bereans tested an apostle by the text: they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And whatever is taught as doctrine on merely human authority is condemned by our Lord Himself — “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).

pos: n. (Johannes Wolleb, 1586–1629, Basel theologian, author of the Compendium of Christian Theology)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan through Latin Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Wolleb, latinised Wollebius, a Basel surname.
biblical_def: Johannes Wolleb taught Old Testament at Basel and wrote a short book that travelled a very long way. His Compendium Theologiae Christianae of 1626 sets out the whole of Reformed doctrine in brief propositions with the proofs attached, in a form a student could carry and memorise, and it was reprinted, translated and used as a textbook from Switzerland to New England; Harvard men read it in the seventeenth century. He died at forty-three. The dictionary names him as the master of the compendium, which is a harder form than it looks. A short systematic theology must decide what belongs, state it so exactly that nothing essential is lost, and leave out the author's own enthusiasms. Done badly it produces a church of slogans; done as Wolleb did it, it gives a young minister a frame on which everything he later learns can be hung, and that is what a compendium is for.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compendium as a brief compilation or composition containing the substance, and epitome as a brief summary.
webster_full: COMPEN'DIUM, n. A brief compilation or composition, containing the principal heads or general principles of a larger work.
EPIT'OME, n. A brief summary; an abridgment; a compendious statement.
TEXT'BOOK, n. A book containing the leading principles of a science, used by students.
PROPOSI'TION, n. A sentence in which something is affirmed or denied.

Heb 6:1
Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,
According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: His short Compendium gave students a frame for the whole of Reformed doctrine and was read as far as New England.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern discomfort with summary itself, which treats any ordered statement of doctrine as a reduction of a living faith to a system. The answer is that every Christian has a system, and the only question is whether it was assembled carefully by better men or accumulated carelessly by himself.

The principle to recover is that sound doctrine has a shape which can be taught, and that the foundation is laid once so that building may proceed. “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13). The writer to the Hebrews assumes the foundation and presses on: “let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation” (Heb 6:1). Paul describes himself as the one who laid it and others as building on it: “as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon” (1Co 3:10). And instruction increases in a man already teachable — “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).

pos: n. (Benedict Aretius, 1505–1574, Bernese professor and commentator on the New Testament)
etymology: Latin Benedictus, blessed; Aretius, a latinisation of the Swiss surname Marti.
biblical_def: Benedict Aretius taught Greek, Hebrew and theology at Bern, wrote commentaries on the whole New Testament that were printed in Geneva and Morges and used widely, and published besides on logic, on the plants of the Alps and on the Bernese church's doctrine. He had a part in the examination of the Italian antitrinitarian Valentino Gentile, who was executed at Bern in 1566 for persistent blasphemy against the Trinity after repeated recantations and relapses. The dictionary states that case rather than hiding it. Bern put a heretic to death, and the dictionary neither pretends otherwise nor applauds it: the civil magistrate's sword is given for the punishment of evildoers, and Reformed Christians have differed, from the sixteenth century to this one, over whether obstinate heresy is among the crimes it may reach. What is not in doubt is the doctrine Gentile denied and Aretius defended, and the entry stands on that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion, and blasphemy as speaking impiously of God.
webster_full: HER'ESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
BLAS'PHEMY, n. An indignity offered to God by words or writing; speaking of God or his attributes impiously.
RECANTA'TION, n. The act of recalling; retraction of a former declaration.
COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: A Bernese commentator who defended the Trinity against Valentino Gentile, executed at Bern in 1566.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is the antitrinitarianism of Gentile and his circle, which denied that the Son is of one essence with the Father and reduced the Trinity to three separable beings of unequal dignity. That is not a variant within Christian orthodoxy; it is a different God. The dictionary names it as the Reformed churches named it, and separately registers that the manner of Bern's answer — death by the magistrate — is a question on which Reformed consciences have not been of one mind, and that the dictionary does not commend it.

The standard is the baptismal formula and the opening of John. “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19) — one name, three Persons. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one” (1Jo 5:7). And the magistrate's office, whatever its proper limits, is itself given by God: he “beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4).

pos: n. (Abraham Musculus, 1534–1591, dean of Bern and defender of the Bernese Reformed settlement)
etymology: Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude; Latin Musculus, a little mouse, latinised from Meusel.
biblical_def: Abraham Musculus was the son of Wolfgang Musculus, the reformer of Augsburg, and he served the church at Bern as pastor and then as dean, which made him the chief minister of the largest Reformed canton in Switzerland. His decades of service fell in the years when Bern was being pressed from one side by Lutheran theologians who wanted the canton to accept the Formula of Concord and its doctrine of the bodily presence in the Supper, and from the other by the growing political weight of a Reformed Geneva whose discipline the Bernese magistrates distrusted. Musculus held the Bernese church to the Second Helvetic Confession through all of it. The dictionary values that holding. A pastor whose whole public work consists in not moving looks, from a distance, as if he did nothing; but a canton that keeps its confession for forty years under pressure from both sides has been kept by somebody, and in Bern it was largely by him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dean as an ecclesiastical dignitary presiding over a body of clergy, and concord as agreement between persons.
webster_full: DEAN, n. An ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral churches, the second in rank; a presiding minister over a body of clergy.
CON'CORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests.
CONFES'SION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
STED'FAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; constant; resolute.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Eph 6:14
Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness;
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
corruption_summary: Forty years holding Bern to the Second Helvetic Confession under pressure from both Lutheran and Genevan directions.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a bias toward movement: we credit the man who changes things and overlook the man whose achievement was that nothing was lost on his watch. Bern could have gone to the Lutheran side on the Supper or to a Genevan polity its magistrates would soon have resented, and it did neither.

The principle to recover is that standing is a labour and is commanded as one. “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58). “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13). The armour is for standing rather than advancing: “Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth” (Eph 6:14). And the profession is to be gripped without wavering, because the faithfulness is God's — “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23).

pos: n. (Markus Rutimeyer, 1580–1647, Bernese theologian and pastor)
etymology: Latin Marcus, of Mars; Swiss German Rutimeyer, the steward of the clearing.
biblical_def: Markus Rutimeyer was a Bernese minister and professor whose working life covered the Thirty Years' War, through which the Swiss cantons kept out of the fighting and were filled instead with refugees and arguments. He preached, taught theology at Bern, took part in the canton's synods, and wrote in defence of the Reformed doctrine of the sacraments against the Lutheran party. The dictionary names him with the Bernese pastors because the Swiss Reformed story in that century is mostly a story of churches that were not destroyed, and such churches leave thin records. Nobody martyred Rutimeyer; no edict closed his church; his canton never had to choose between apostasy and exile. He catechised, preached, buried, disciplined and taught for forty years in a settled Reformed commonwealth, which is what every persecuted church in Europe was praying for, and it is worth naming the men who had it and used it well.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines settled as established, and catechise as to instruct by asking questions and receiving answers.
webster_full: SET'TLED, pp. Established; fixed; determined; composed; quiet.
CAT'ECHISE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions and receiving answers, and by correcting the answers.
COM'MONWEALTH, n. An established form of government; the whole body of people in a state.
SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council; a meeting of ministers and elders.

And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Psa 16:6
The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
corruption_summary: Forty years of ordinary ministry in a settled Reformed canton while Europe burned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is an appetite for crisis, which teaches Christians that only the besieged church is a serious church, and leaves those in quiet places feeling that nothing is happening. Rutimeyer's Bern was quiet while Germany lost a third of its people, and quiet was a mercy to be used rather than a reproach.

The principle to recover is that peace is a thing to pray for and a setting in which the church grows. We are to pray for rulers “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). The result of rest is explicitly growth: “Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified” (Act 9:31). Even exiles are told to seek the peace of the city they are in: “seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives” (Jer 29:7). And the man given a quiet lot may say what the psalmist said — “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places” (Psa 16:6).

pos: n. (Johann Rudolf Stucki, 1596–1660, Zurich professor of theology and Hebrew)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Germanic Rudolf, famous wolf; Stucki, a Zurich surname.
biblical_def: Johann Rudolf Stucki belonged to a Zurich family that supplied the city's church and school with ministers and professors across several generations, and he taught Hebrew and then theology at the Carolinum, Zurich's academy. He was one of the men who carried Zurich's part in the Reformed correspondence of the mid-seventeenth century and who trained the generation that produced Heidegger and Hottinger. The dictionary names him for the teaching rather than for a book. A city church that produces scholars for a century and a half does so because someone is standing in front of boys with a Hebrew grammar every morning, and the names of such men survive mostly in matriculation registers and in the dedications of their pupils' books. Zurich's long theological fruitfulness — from Zwingli and Bullinger through to Heidegger and the Hottingers — was a matter of unbroken teaching, and Stucki held one of its unglamorous middle links.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines professor as one who teaches a science in a university, and succession as a following of one thing after another in order.
webster_full: PROFESS'OR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; the occupant of a chair in a university.
SUCCES'SION, n. A following of things in order; the act of following in order; a series of persons or things.
ACAD'EMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
DISCI'PLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: A middle link in Zurich's unbroken chain of teaching, from Zwingli and Bullinger to Heidegger and Hottinger.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the great-man reading of church history, which remembers the men who wrote the confessions and forgets that each of them was taught Hebrew by somebody. Zurich's productivity over a hundred and fifty years was not a succession of geniuses; it was a school that kept going.

The principle to recover is that God works by generations and commands the handing on. “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — four links in one sentence. “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4). The words are to be first in the teacher's own heart: “these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6). And the teachable man gains by it — “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).

pos: n. (Johann Ludwig Fabricius, 1632–1697, Swiss-born theologian and professor at Heidelberg)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Germanic Ludwig, famous in war; Latin Fabricius, a craftsman, a smith.
biblical_def: Johann Ludwig Fabricius was born at Schaffhausen, trained in the Swiss and Dutch schools, and spent the bulk of his career at Heidelberg, where he taught theology and served the Palatine church in the generation after the Thirty Years' War had ruined it. Heidelberg had been sacked, its library carried off to Rome, its university closed for years; Fabricius belonged to the men who restarted it. He was known for a moderate temper in controversy and was consulted on the delicate question of whether the Palatinate should employ scholars of doubtful orthodoxy in philosophy. The dictionary records him as a rebuilder. There is a kind of service that consists in reopening a school whose books are gone, in a city that has been burned twice, for students whose fathers were killed; it produces no famous treatise and it decides whether a church exists in fifty years. Fabricius gave his life to it, and the Heidelberg Catechism went on being taught because men like him reopened the lecture rooms.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rebuild as to build again what has been demolished, and restore as to bring back to a former good state.
webster_full: REBUILD', v.t. To build again; to renew a structure; to rebuild a house or a wall.
RESTO'RE, v.t. To bring back; to return; to bring back to a former and better state.
RU'IN, n. Destruction; overthrow; the remains of a decayed or demolished building.
UNIVERS'ITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students.
scriptures: Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.

Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing?

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
corruption_summary: He helped reopen Heidelberg's ruined university and church after the Thirty Years' War.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a preference for founding over rebuilding. Founders get the credit; the men who reopen a burned institution with no library, no endowment and half a faculty are remembered, if at all, as caretakers. In the history of the church the second work is far commoner and quite as necessary.

The principle to recover is that God calls His people to build again on ruins and promises to use them in it: “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach” (Neh 2:17). The promise is explicit: “And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12). The second temple looked like nothing beside the first, and the question was asked aloud — “Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory?” (Hag 2:3) — and the answer came: “who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10).
